_meta.note: Regression reference for Name That Feeling, re-recorded after the 2026-09-04 word-quality + ambiguity-preservation correction pass. v2 baseline (4 cases) is superseded — schema gained a 4th match value (NO ADEQUATE MATCH) and best_match.word/language/pronunciation/definition may now be empty. Re-run with `npm run check:golden name-that-feeling` against a local backend. What to read for by eye, since no gate can see it: (1) best_match.word must fit the CENTRAL, ordinary meaning of the feeling described, never an obscure/archaic sense smuggling in an unstated element (guilt, resentment, wrongdoing); (2) no named emotional ambiguity (envy, comparison, guilt, etc.) the visitor flagged as unclear may be resolved into a flat fact — the visitor's own uncertainty must survive; (3) no claim about what the visitor or someone in their story 'knew' unless it traces to the visitor's own supplied context; (4) best_match.match is never STRONG/CLOSE/PARTIAL for a phrase that isn't a real, findable word — a coined phrase belongs in made_up_name or as an empty-fielded NO ADEQUATE MATCH; (5) share_line's framing (There's a word for / One word that comes close is / This reminds me of / There may not be one word for this) must match the match enum exactly. Each case carries its own `guards` line. See audit/tool-notes/NAMETHATFEELING-NOTES.md.

cases.name: vacation-nostalgia-close-match

input.description: That feeling on the last day of a vacation where I am happy I went, sad it is ending, and somehow already nostalgic for it before I am even home. It happens every time, even on short trips.
input.context: Happens most when the place felt like somewhere I could have lived.

cases.guards: The reference case this rewrite exists for. best_match.match should read CLOSE MATCH or PARTIAL, not STRONG, since the timing (missing it while still there) is not what the classic word usually means — where_it_doesnt must name that gap explicitly, not stay silent because the match otherwise sounds good. No 'only Portuguese people feel this,' no 'the mark of someone who...', no invented etymology. made_up_name.useful may legitimately be false here if an established word or phrase already covers it — do not force a coined term to fill the field.

ingredients: happiness that the experience happened
sadness that it is ending
nostalgia for it while still in it
this pattern repeating regardless of trip length

best_match.definition: A simultaneous mixture of pleasure and pain; happiness tinged with sadness or regret.
best_match.where_it_doesnt: Bittersweet does not inherently capture the element of anticipatory nostalgia — the feeling of missing something before you have even left it. It names the pleasure-and-pain mix but not the temporal strangeness of being homesick for a place you are still in.

other_words.definition: Longing mixed with sadness or mild regret; a yearning for something absent or past.
other_words.captures: The longing for the place and the sadness about leaving. The sense of already missing it.
other_words.misses: Does not capture the happiness you also felt about the experience itself. Wistfulness leans melancholic; your feeling includes genuine joy.

other_words.definition: Deeply moving; touching the emotions in a way that is sharp or bittersweet.
other_words.captures: The intensity of feeling multiple things at once — the sharpness of that last day when happiness and sadness collide.

output.plain_english: Happy the trip happened, sad it is ending, and already nostalgic for it while still there.
output.share_line: There's a word for that particular ache on the last day: bittersweet. It captures the happiness and sadness at once. The part that catches you before you even leave — that premature nostalgia — is what makes it sharp.

cases.name: rootless-displacement-made-up-name

input.description: I moved away from my hometown years ago and built a whole life somewhere else. Sometimes I feel homesick for a place that does not really exist anymore, and I am not sure I would even fit there now. It is not quite grief and not quite nostalgia.
input.context: What was happening: thinking about visiting for the holidays. Anything important: I have moved countries twice and feel a bit unmoored between places.

cases.guards: The exact shape of feeling ('displacement,' 'unmoored between countries') that invites culture-stereotyping and personality-reading in the old tool. Nothing may say 'only expats understand this,' 'this culture has a word because...', or attribute the feeling to what kind of person the visitor is. Any Portuguese/German/etc. word offered must carry a real, honest definition — no invented etymology or pronunciation offered without genuine confidence.

ingredients: Longing for a place from your past
Awareness that the place has changed
Uncertainty about whether you belong there now
Being caught between homes
what_you_described.tension: You miss something real, but you also know it no longer exists in the form you remember — and you are not sure you fit into what it has become. The homesickness is partly for a place, partly for a version of yourself that may not exist there anymore.

best_match.definition: The state of being separated from a place, culture, or way of life you belonged to; also, the condition of being between places without settling fully into either.
best_match.why_it_fits: Displacement names the core of what you described: you are physically absent from your hometown and emotionally unmoored between places. It captures the sense of not quite belonging anywhere right now — not quite home in your new country, not quite at home in your hometown anymore. It is less about sadness than about spatial and emotional dislocation.
best_match.where_it_doesnt: Displacement emphasizes the absence and disconnection more than the specific longing or nostalgia you feel when you think about visiting. It is also sometimes used clinically for displacement of populations; the emotional meaning is real but less commonly used this way.

other_words.definition: The experience of not fully belonging to or fitting into any single place or culture; existing in a liminal space between homes.
other_words.captures: The feeling of living outside any clear home base, which fits your experience of moving countries twice and feeling unmoored. It explicitly names the in-between rather than the longing itself.
other_words.misses: Does not capture the specific homesickness you feel — the pull backward toward something that no longer exists as you remember it.

other_words.definition: Longing for a version of a place that has changed so much you cannot quite return to it; nostalgia for something that no longer materially exists.
other_words.captures: The odd quality of your homesickness — you are missing a place that is no longer there in the form you knew. It names the gap between the hometown you remember and the hometown that exists now.
other_words.misses: Does not address the uncertainty about your own fit, or the broader sense of being between places. Focuses narrowly on the nostalgia for what was.

output.plain_english: Homesick for a place that has changed, uncertain whether you would fit there anymore, and caught between countries — missing something that partly exists in memory more than geography.
output.share_line: One word that comes close is displacement — it names the homesickness and the disorientation of being caught between places, though it does not quite capture the specific longing for something that no longer exists as you remember it.

cases.name: schadenfreude-strong-match-sparse

input.description: That little flicker of satisfaction when someone who was rude to me gets stuck in traffic right after.

cases.guards: A well-known, easily-matched feeling with NO context supplied — nothing may invent a target audience, backstory, or reason for the feeling beyond what was said. If the match is genuinely strong (schadenfreude or equivalent), where_it_doesnt may legitimately be empty — must not manufacture a caveat just to fill the field. share_line must use 'There's a word for...' ONLY if match is STRONG MATCH; if the model instead returns CLOSE MATCH, share_line must use 'One word that comes close is...' instead — the two must agree.

ingredients: A small, immediate moment of satisfaction
Directed at someone who was rude to you
Triggered by their misfortune (traffic jam)
A sense of poetic justice or fitting consequence
what_you_described.tension: Satisfaction at another's minor hardship, which most people would not admit openly — a small, guilty pleasure that feels both petty and somehow earned.

best_match.definition: Pleasure or satisfaction derived from another person's misfortune, especially when that misfortune feels deserved or proportional.
best_match.why_it_fits: You felt a flicker of satisfaction when the rude person hit a concrete consequence. That is exactly what schadenfreude names — the small, immediate pleasure in seeing someone experience a fitting setback. The word does not require the misfortune to be severe; a traffic jam counts. It does not require vindictiveness; a flicker is enough.

other_words.definition: A small sense of gratification that one might not fully admit to, often tied to something trivial but felt keenly.
other_words.captures: The lightness and smallness of what you felt — a flicker, not a roaring satisfaction. Also captures the faint awareness that it is petty.
other_words.misses: Does not name the specific shape: that the satisfaction comes from someone else's misfortune. Schadenfreude marks that as the whole point.

other_words.definition: A punishment or fate that someone deserves, especially as a natural or fitting consequence.
other_words.captures: The sense that the traffic was fitting — a just, if small, consequence for rudeness. This is what satisfied you.
other_words.misses: Names the event, not your feeling about it. You felt satisfied; comeuppance describes what happened. The satisfaction came from seeing it arrive.

output.plain_english: A small, guilty pleasure in seeing someone rude experience a minor misfortune that feels like a fitting consequence.
output.share_line: There's a word for that small, immediate satisfaction when someone who was unkind hits a fitting setback: schadenfreude.

cases.name: social-fatigue-prefer-english

input.description: The specific tiredness of small talk with someone I don't actually want to talk to, where I have to perform interest I don't feel.
input.context: What was happening: a work event where I had to network. Anything important: it's not social anxiety, just exhaustion from faking engagement.

cases.guards: Tests 'prefer a familiar English phrase over an impressive foreign word that only loosely matches.' If the honest best answer is an ordinary English phrase, best_match.language should legitimately read 'English' rather than the model reaching for an exotic foreign word merely for novelty — do not treat a foreign-language result on this case as a bug on its own, but do check that whichever word is chosen is not stretched to fit better than it genuinely does.

ingredients: exhaustion from sustained performance
faking interest you do not feel
obligation to continue the interaction
the specific drain of small talk
what_you_described.tension: You are engaged in the interaction (you cannot leave) while simultaneously disengaged from it (you do not want to be there). The tiredness comes from holding both states at once.

best_match.where_it_doesnt: No single established word captures the specific exhaustion of sustained fake engagement during small talk. Words like 'fatigue' or 'weariness' name tiredness but not the performance. 'Burnout' suggests longer-term depletion. 'Feigned interest' names what you are doing but not how it feels. The feeling lives in the gap between those.

other_words.definition: the depletion that comes from sustained social interaction, especially when it requires emotional labor or performance
other_words.captures: the exhaustion specific to social settings and the cost of sustained engagement
other_words.misses: does not necessarily imply that you are faking interest rather than simply depleted by genuine socializing; does not capture the particular drain of small talk with someone you actively do not want to talk to

other_words.definition: superficial conversation you are expected to maintain despite lack of genuine interest
other_words.captures: the forced nature of the interaction and the specificity of small talk
other_words.misses: names what you are doing, not how it feels; does not capture the tiredness or the performance

other_words.definition: concealing your actual emotional state or interests to meet social expectations
other_words.captures: the performance aspect—hiding disinterest behind performed interest
other_words.misses: does not specifically address tiredness or the particular drain of small talk; carries different connotations in different contexts

output.plain_english: The specific exhaustion of having to pretend interest in a conversation you do not want to be having.
output.share_line: There may not be one word for this, but here's how it feels: the specific exhaustion of having to pretend interest in a conversation you do not want to be having.

cases.name: friend-good-news-dont-resolve-ambiguity

input.description: A friend told me their good news and I felt something drop before I felt happy for them. The happy part was real. So was the other part, and I don't have a word for it that isn't just 'jealous', which isn't quite right either.
input.context: They deserved it completely and I'd have been upset for them if it hadn't happened. It passed in about a minute. I still think about it.

cases.guards: The exact live bug report that produced 'compunction' as a strained primary match plus a string of invented specifics (the friend 'deserved' it stated as the tool's own conclusion rather than the visitor's, 'a flash of your own lack', 'authentic joy... took over'). PRIMARY MATCH RULE: best_match.word must fit the CENTRAL, ordinary meaning of the description — not an obscure/archaic sense that smuggles in an unstated element (guilt, wrongdoing, resentment). DON'T RESOLVE THE AMBIGUITY: nothing may declare the first feeling WAS or WASN'T envy/comparison/personal lack as a flat fact the model decided — the visitor's own uncertainty must survive into the answer (e.g. 'the description doesn't establish which'). Any claim that the visitor 'knew' something (like the friend deserving it) must trace to the visitor's OWN supplied context, not be invented — check it's grounded in the context field before treating it as a violation.

ingredients: An immediate physical or emotional drop
Genuine happiness for your friend that followed
Uncertainty about what the first sensation was
The fact that both feelings were real and coexisted
what_you_described.tension: You felt something like loss or lack before the happiness arrived — and you can't name the first part without claiming envy, which doesn't fit the whole picture.

best_match.definition: A sudden sharp feeling of pain, regret, longing, or acute disappointment — often brief and without a clear cause.
best_match.why_it_fits: A pang describes that sudden drop you felt, the sharpness of it, and its brevity. It does not require you to name what caused it. You don't need to know whether it was disappointment, longing, comparison, or something else — pang holds the shape of the sensation itself without deciding its source.
best_match.where_it_doesnt: Pang often carries a sense of regret or missing something, which may or may not match what you experienced. It does not by itself resolve what that drop was made of.

other_words.definition: A brief, uncertain flash of feeling or doubt — something that appears and fades quickly.
other_words.captures: The speed and transience of what you felt. The sense that it was there and then gone.
other_words.misses: Flicker is lighter and more tentative than what you described — your feeling was sharp enough that you still think about it. Pang better names the intensity.

other_words.definition: A sharp, sudden, and usually brief feeling of pain, regret, or doubt.
other_words.captures: The sudden, physical quality of the drop. The way it arrived before you could name it.
other_words.misses: Twinge leans slightly more toward physical sensation than emotional. It can suggest regret more strongly than pang does, which may or may not match your experience.

output.plain_english: You felt a sharp drop the moment you heard the news — something immediate and physical — before the happiness arrived. Both were real. The drop lasted about a minute. You still think about what it was.
output.share_line: One word that comes close is a pang — that sudden drop before happiness, sharp and real, without needing to name exactly what caused it.

cases.name: meeting-mispronunciation-no-adequate-match

input.description: The specific discomfort of watching someone confidently mispronounce a word in a meeting and deciding in that half-second whether correcting them is worth the awkwardness it will cause everyone else in the room.

cases.guards: Tests the new NO ADEQUATE MATCH pathway end to end (PRIMARY MATCH RULE's 'prefer NO EXACT WORD over an impressive but semantically strained answer'). If match comes back NO ADEQUATE MATCH: best_match.word/language/pronunciation/definition should be empty rather than a coined phrase / meta-statement about the absence dressed up as a candidate ('No established single word', 'the discomfort of a no-win moment') — cleanNoMatchWord strips exactly that pattern server-side (check-golden can't see this by structure alone; eyeball it). where_it_doesnt becomes essential in this case and must say plainly what's missing. plain_english must stand on its own as the real answer. share_line must use the NO ADEQUATE MATCH framing ('There may not be one word for this...'). This case may instead legitimately come back CLOSE or PARTIAL MATCH with a real short phrase (e.g. 'caught between') — either outcome is fine as long as word/match/where_it_doesnt stay internally consistent.

ingredients: Recognition that someone has made an error
Awareness of their confidence despite the error
A split-second decision point with competing costs
Concern about creating awkwardness for others in the room
The discomfort of the moment itself — the pause, the calculation
what_you_described.tension: You are caught between two kinds of awkwardness: the awkwardness of letting an error pass uncorrected versus the awkwardness of correcting it and drawing attention to the mistake in front of everyone.

best_match.where_it_doesnt: No single established word captures the full shape of this: the specific discomfort of the split-second calculation, the collision between accuracy and social grace, the audience awareness, and the paralysis of choice. The moment has too many moving parts for a single word to hold.

other_words.definition: Placed in a difficult position with no good option
other_words.captures: The bind itself — you cannot move in either direction without cost
other_words.misses: Does not name the specific social calculation or the speed of the decision point

other_words.definition: A visceral discomfort at an awkward social moment
other_words.captures: The physical sensation of the discomfort, the social dimension
other_words.misses: Usually describes witnessing awkwardness, not the internal calculation of whether to create it

other_words.definition: Left in suspense or uncertainty; unable to proceed
other_words.captures: The half-second freeze, the moment before action
other_words.misses: Does not capture the strategic element — that you are weighing options, not simply stuck

output.plain_english: That half-second where you spot an error, notice they are confident about it, and instantly weigh whether correcting them is worth the social cost of making it public in front of everyone watching.
output.share_line: There may not be one word for this, but here's how it feels: that half-second where you spot an error, notice they are confident about it, and instantly weigh whether correcting them is worth the social cost of making it public in front of everyone watching.
